new_text: "Adèle," I asked, "who did you live with when you were in that pretty, clean town you mentioned?"
Adèle sang the little song tunefully enough, with the innocence of her age. When she finished, she hopped off my knee and said, "Now, Mademoiselle, I will recite some poetry for you."

After breakfast, Adèle and I went to the library, which Mr. Rochester had designated as the schoolroom. Most of the books were locked behind glass doors, but one bookcase stood open, containing all the elementary works needed, plus several volumes of lighter reading—poetry, biography, travel books, a few novels, and so on. He had probably decided that these were all a governess would need for her own reading, and indeed they more than satisfied me for now. Compared to the meager pickings I had occasionally managed at Lowood, they seemed a rich harvest of entertainment and knowledge. The room also held a cabinet piano, brand new and of excellent quality, as well as an easel for painting and a pair of globes.
The conversation turned to Adèle and continued until we reached the bright, cheerful lower floor. Adèle came running to meet us in the hall, calling out—

This, as an aside, will strike some as cold language—people who hold solemn beliefs about the angelic nature of children and the duty of their teachers to worship them with blind devotion. But I am not writing to flatter parental vanity, to echo platitudes, or to prop up pretense. I am simply telling the truth. I felt a genuine concern for Adèle's welfare and progress, and a quiet liking for the child herself—just as I felt toward Mrs. Fairfax a gratitude for her kindness and a pleasure in her company proportional to the calm regard she had for me and the moderation of her mind and character.

Anyone who wants to can blame me when I add that, now and then, when I walked alone in the grounds, or went down to the gates and looked along the road, or when, while Adèle played with her nurse and Mrs. Fairfax made preserves in the storeroom, I climbed the three staircases, pushed open the attic trapdoor, and stood on the roof looking out over the secluded fields, the hills, and the dim horizon—that then I longed for a power of vision that could reach beyond that boundary, that could see the busy world, the towns, the regions full of life I had heard of but never witnessed. That then I craved more practical experience than I possessed, more contact with my fellow human beings, more acquaintance with the variety of human character than was within my reach here. I valued what was good in Mrs. Fairfax and in Adèle, but I believed in the existence of other, more vivid kinds of goodness, and I wanted to see what I believed in.

October, November, and December passed. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adèle because she had a cold. Since Adèle backed the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious holidays had been in my own childhood, I agreed, thinking it right to be flexible. It was a fine, calm day, though very cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library all morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that needed posting, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and volunteered to carry it to Hay—a pleasant two-mile walk on a winter afternoon. After settling Adèle comfortably in her little chair by Mrs. Fairfax's fire, giving her the best wax doll (which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer) and a storybook for variety, and answering her "Come back soon, my dear friend, my darling Mademoiselle Jeannette" with a kiss, I set out.

The hall was neither dark nor fully lit—only the high-hung bronze lamp illuminated it, plus a warm glow that suffused both the hall and the lower steps of the oak staircase. This ruddy light came from the great dining room, whose double doors stood open, showing a cheerful fire in the grate gleaming on the marble hearth and brass fire tools and casting the most pleasant radiance over the purple curtains and polished furniture. It also revealed a group near the mantelpiece. I had barely glimpsed them, and barely registered a cheerful mix of voices among which I thought I heard Adèle's, when the door was closed.
"Yes, and Miss Adèle. They're in the dining room. John has gone for the surgeon—the master has had an accident. His horse fell and his ankle is sprained."
